tier_reason: STATUS compares libzahl against GMP, TomsFastMath and LibTomMath on 1 to 4097-bit operands, and names the CPU (Intel Core 2 Quad Q9300), the compilers (gcc and clang with glibc/musl) and the flags (-O3 tested as 'Good'; config.mk CFLAGS -std=c99 -O3 -flto, which the Makefile's benchmark targets use). The benchmark code is public in bench/benchmark-func.c and bench/benchmark.c, with per-library translation layers such as bench/libgmp.h. It meets A by the rubric, but the published result is a per-function ranking with crossover sizes, not timing tables, and no compiler or GMP versions are given.

corrections.claimed_speedup: STATUS (1-4097 bits): zset, zswap, zbtest, zsave, zload, zneg(a,b), zabs(a,b), ztrunc(a,b,c), znot, zbits and zcmpu are 'always fastest'; zsub is 'always fastest'; zadd is 'fastest after ~90 (clang), ~260 (gcc+musl), or ~840 (gcc+glibc)'; zand and zor are fastest only after ~400 and ~1150 bits. Losses: zlsh is 'not too fast anymore'; for zrsh 'gmp is almost always faster'; zmul, zsqr and zstr are 'slowest'; for zstr_length(a,10) 'gmp is faster'. The 'zgcd 21 % of gmp' row sits in the file's '[out of date legacy area]' (152-bit operands), and the file uses 'X % of Y' in rows that still need optimising, so it most likely means libzahl is slower than GMP there.
corrections.caveats: Mixed result, not a general win over GMP. The STATUS file's own multiply, square and string-conversion rows say 'slowest', and GMP wins on right shift. Results are published only as per-function rankings and crossover sizes, with no timing tables. Measured on a 2008 Core 2 Quad with no CPU extensions, so modern GMP assembly paths (mulx, adx, AVX) are not represented. Compiler and GMP versions are not stated, and the GMP numbers come through the repo's translation layer (bench/libgmp.h). STATUS notes that GMP does no failure checking while libzahl does, that TomsFastMath has a compile-time size limit, and that the author flags some rows (zlsb, zcmp) as suspicious. The gcd figure comes from an out-of-date legacy section. Repository archived 2024-10-06; last commit 2022-07-20. The README itself gives no numbers.

notes: Metadata confirmed on the GitHub page: ISC, archived 2024-10-06, not a fork, 32 stars, last commit 2022-07-20. The record was accurate, apart from presenting the legacy 'zgcd 21 % of gmp' line without context; the catalog should present this as a narrow win on cheap operations (assignment, sign, compare, add/sub at larger sizes), not on multiply or division.

tier_reason: These are first-party numbers from the project's own benchmarks/bench_compare.c, which uses loop-carried add/mul/div over 10M iterations against GCC __float128. No CPU model or compiler version is given for the published runs; the Google Benchmark output shows only '12 X 3266.69 MHz'. The flags can be inferred only from CMakeLists.txt, so this is C.

corrections.claimed_speedup: The README has two inconsistent tables for the same 10M-iteration latency test against __float128 (GCC). The summary table gives __float128 add 152.31 ms, mul 189.81 ms, div 276.00 ms, and simd-f128 73.60, 56.15 and 159.70 ms; it claims '3.38x faster than GCC' on multiply and '1.7x to 3.3x faster' overall. The 'Comparative Speed' section with raw bench_compare console output gives __float128 153.37 / 193.23 / 325.37 ms and simd-f128 (AVX2) 99.44 / 74.46 / 207.98 ms, which it states as 'multiplication is 2.59x faster, addition is 1.54x faster, and division is 1.56x faster'.
corrections.compiler_and_flags: Not stated for the published runs. CMakeLists.txt sets -Wall -Wextra -O3 for GCC/Clang, plus -mavx2 -mfma when SIMD_F128_AVX2 is on (inferred from the build files, not from the benchmark write-up).
corrections.caveats: Weak evidence. No CPU model or compiler version is given (the Google Benchmark output shows only 12 x 3266.69 MHz with a 16 MiB L3). The README's two benchmark tables disagree (multiply 3.38x vs 2.59x; division 1.73x vs 1.56x, derived from page data), so the headline '1.7x to 3.3x' comes from the more favourable run. The comparison is against __float128, not GMP or MPFR (the README only calls GMP/MPFR 'Very Slow', with no numbers). Double-double (~106-bit mantissa) is not IEEE binary128: it has a smaller exponent range and no correct rounding, and the README warns of catastrophic cancellation and says to use __float128 when binary128 compliance is needed. In the Google Benchmark mul loop (bench_arithmetic.cpp) the value is multiplied by about 2 every iteration, so it overflows to infinity quickly. The project is very new (first commits 2026-08-09) and has 2 stars.
